CHAPTER 12 - WAVE PHENOMENA

Introduction

A wave is a disturbance that travels through a medium (or through space) transporting energy and momentum from one place to another WITHOUT any net transport of the medium itself. When you drop a stone in a pond, ripples spread outward, but a floating leaf merely bobs up and down - it is the disturbance, not the water, that moves away. Sound, light, ripples on water, waves on a stretched string and seismic waves are all examples of wave motion. This chapter builds the language of waves, derives the key relations that govern them, and applies these ideas to strings, air columns, beats and the Doppler effect.

12.1 WAVE MOTION AND TYPES OF WAVES

In a mechanical wave the particles of the medium oscillate about their mean (equilibrium) positions while the energy is handed on from particle to particle. Two features are essential for a mechanical wave: (i) the medium must have INERTIA (mass, so it can store kinetic energy) and (ii) it must have ELASTICITY (a restoring force that brings a displaced particle back). Waves are classified by the direction in which the particles vibrate relative to the direction the wave travels.

TRANSVERSE WAVES: the particles of the medium vibrate PERPENDICULAR to the direction of wave propagation. A wave on a stretched string, ripples on water and all electromagnetic waves (light) are transverse. Transverse mechanical waves need a medium that can support shear, so they travel through solids and along surfaces but not through the bulk of a gas or a liquid. A transverse wave shows CRESTS (points of maximum upward displacement) and TROUGHS (points of maximum downward displacement).

LONGITUDINAL WAVES: the particles vibrate PARALLEL to (along) the direction of propagation. Sound in air is the standard example. Here the medium is alternately squeezed and stretched, forming regions of COMPRESSION (particles crowded together, high pressure) and RAREFACTION (particles far apart, low pressure). Longitudinal waves can travel through solids, liquids and gases because all three resist compression.

12.2 TERMS THAT DESCRIBE A WAVE

AMPLITUDE (A): the maximum displacement of a particle from its mean position. It is measured in metres and is linked to the energy carried by the wave (energy is proportional to A^2).
WAVELENGTH (lambda): the distance between two consecutive points that are in the same phase - crest to crest, or trough to trough, or compression to compression. Measured in metres.
TIME PERIOD (T): the time taken by one particle to complete one full oscillation. Measured in seconds.
FREQUENCY (f or nu): the number of complete oscillations made by a particle per second, f = 1/T. Measured in hertz (Hz).
WAVE VELOCITY (v): the distance travelled by the disturbance per second. In one time period T the wave advances by exactly one wavelength lambda, so

   v = lambda / T = f lambda .

This single relation, v = f lambda, connects the three basic quantities and is used constantly. For a given medium v is (nearly) fixed, so a higher frequency automatically means a shorter wavelength.

Worked example: A tuning fork of frequency 512 Hz sends sound through air where v = 340 m/s. The wavelength is lambda = v/f = 340/512 = 0.664 m.

12.3 THE PROGRESSIVE (TRAVELLING) WAVE EQUATION

A progressive wave carries energy steadily forward. Consider a wave travelling in the +x direction. If the particle at x = 0 executes simple harmonic motion y = A sin(omega t), then a particle at position x repeats that same motion but a little LATER, because the disturbance needs time x/v to reach it. The displacement of the particle at x at time t is therefore

   y(x, t) = A sin(omega t - k x)

where omega = 2 pi f is the ANGULAR FREQUENCY (rad/s) and k is the ANGULAR WAVE NUMBER (also called the propagation constant),

   k = 2 pi / lambda   (rad/m).

The quantity (omega t - k x) is the PHASE of the wave. The wave speed follows directly from these definitions: v = omega/k = (2 pi f)/(2 pi/lambda) = f lambda, in agreement with 12.2. A wave moving in the -x direction is written y = A sin(omega t + k x). The maximum speed of a PARTICLE of the medium is v_particle(max) = A omega, which is quite different from the WAVE speed v - do not confuse the two.

Worked example: For y = 0.02 sin(300 t - 5 x) (SI units), omega = 300 rad/s and k = 5 rad/m. Then f = omega/2pi = 47.7 Hz, lambda = 2pi/k = 1.257 m, and v = omega/k = 300/5 = 60 m/s. The amplitude is 0.02 m.

12.4 SPEED OF A WAVE ON A STRETCHED STRING

The speed of a transverse wave on a string depends only on the properties of the string, not on its frequency. If T is the tension (in newtons) and mu is the LINEAR MASS DENSITY (mass per unit length, kg/m), then

   v = sqrt(T / mu) .

A tighter string (larger T) carries waves faster; a heavier string (larger mu) carries them slower. This is why the thin, tight strings of a guitar sound higher than the thick, slack ones.

Worked example: A string of length 1 m has mass 20 g, so mu = 0.020/1.0 = 0.02 kg/m. Stretched to a tension T = 80 N, the wave speed is v = sqrt(80/0.02) = sqrt(4000) = 63.2 m/s.

12.5 SPEED OF SOUND IN A GAS - NEWTON'S FORMULA AND LAPLACE'S CORRECTION

Newton reasoned that sound is an elastic wave and proposed that the speed of sound in a gas is v = sqrt(E/rho), where E is the elasticity and rho the density. He assumed the compressions and rarefactions happen SLOWLY enough for the temperature to stay constant (an ISOTHERMAL process), so E equals the pressure P:

   Newton:  v = sqrt(P / rho).

For air at normal conditions this gives about 280 m/s - roughly 15 percent too low compared with the measured 332 m/s. Laplace corrected the reasoning: sound compressions and rarefactions occur so RAPIDLY that no heat can flow in or out (an ADIABATIC process). For an adiabatic change the effective elasticity is gamma P, where gamma = C_p/C_v is the ratio of the specific heats. Hence

   Laplace:  v = sqrt(gamma P / rho).

For air gamma = 1.40, and this raises the predicted speed to about 332 m/s, in excellent agreement with experiment. Using P = rho R T / M one can also write v = sqrt(gamma R T / M), showing that the speed of sound in a gas depends on temperature (rises with sqrt(T)) but not on pressure (since P/rho stays constant at fixed T).

12.6 PRINCIPLE OF SUPERPOSITION

When two or more waves travel through the same region at the same time, the resultant displacement of a particle at any instant is the VECTOR (algebraic) SUM of the displacements that each wave would produce on its own:

   y = y1 + y2 + ... 

After they have crossed, each wave continues unchanged, as if the others had never been there. This principle of superposition is the foundation of interference, stationary waves and beats.

12.7 INTERFERENCE OF WAVES

When two waves of the SAME frequency and a constant phase relationship (coherent waves) overlap, the steady pattern of reinforcement and cancellation that results is called INTERFERENCE.
 - CONSTRUCTIVE interference: the waves arrive IN PHASE (path difference = n lambda, n = 0, 1, 2, ...). Crest falls on crest; the amplitudes add and the resultant is loud/bright. Maximum amplitude = A1 + A2.
 - DESTRUCTIVE interference: the waves arrive OUT OF PHASE by half a cycle (path difference = (n + 1/2) lambda). Crest falls on trough; the amplitudes subtract and the resultant is faint/dark. Minimum amplitude = |A1 - A2|.
Because intensity is proportional to (amplitude)^2, interference merely REDISTRIBUTES energy from the dark regions into the bright ones - total energy is conserved.

12.8 STATIONARY (STANDING) WAVES

When two progressive waves of the same amplitude and frequency travel in OPPOSITE directions (for example an incident wave and its reflection) and superpose, they form a STATIONARY WAVE. Adding y1 = A sin(omega t - k x) and y2 = A sin(omega t + k x) gives

   y = 2 A cos(k x) sin(omega t).

The wave no longer travels; every particle vibrates in SHM with an amplitude 2A cos(kx) that depends on its position x. Certain points never move - these are the NODES (amplitude zero, where cos kx = 0, spaced lambda/2 apart). Halfway between the nodes are the ANTINODES (amplitude a maximum 2A). The distance between a node and the next antinode is lambda/4. No energy is transported past a node, so a stationary wave stores energy rather than carrying it away.

12.9 VIBRATIONS OF STRINGS - HARMONICS AND OVERTONES

A string fixed at both ends must have a NODE at each end. The simplest pattern (the FUNDAMENTAL or first harmonic) has just one antinode in the middle; then the length L holds half a wavelength, L = lambda/2, so lambda = 2L and the fundamental frequency is

   f1 = v/(2L) = (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu).

Higher modes fit an integer number of half-wavelengths: L = n lambda_n/2, giving f_n = n f1 for n = 1, 2, 3, .... These are the HARMONICS. The fundamental is the first harmonic; f2 = 2 f1 is the second harmonic (first overtone); f3 = 3 f1 is the third harmonic (second overtone), and so on. A string can sound ALL integer harmonics.

12.10 VIBRATIONS OF AIR COLUMNS - OPEN AND CLOSED PIPES

An OPEN PIPE (open at both ends) has a displacement ANTINODE at each open end. The fundamental fits half a wavelength, L = lambda/2, so f1 = v/(2L); the allowed frequencies are f_n = n v/(2L) with n = 1, 2, 3, .... An open pipe, like a string, produces ALL harmonics (both odd and even).

A CLOSED PIPE (closed at one end, open at the other) has a NODE at the closed end and an ANTINODE at the open end. The fundamental fits a quarter wavelength, L = lambda/4, so f1 = v/(4L). The allowed frequencies are f_n = (2n - 1) v/(4L) = v/4L, 3v/4L, 5v/4L, ... - i.e. ONLY the ODD harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, ...). For the same length, a closed pipe sounds an octave LOWER than an open pipe because its fundamental v/4L is half of v/2L.

Worked example: A closed pipe 0.5 m long in air (v = 340 m/s) has fundamental f1 = 340/(4 x 0.5) = 170 Hz; its next allowed frequency (third harmonic) is 3 x 170 = 510 Hz.

12.11 BEATS

When two notes of SLIGHTLY DIFFERENT frequencies f1 and f2 sound together, the loudness rises and falls periodically. These regular waxings and wanings of intensity are BEATS. Superposing the two waves shows that the amplitude is modulated at a rate equal to the DIFFERENCE of the frequencies, so the number of beats heard per second (the BEAT FREQUENCY) is

   f_beat = |f1 - f2|.

Beats are audible only when the two frequencies are close (within about 10 Hz), otherwise the ear hears two separate notes. Musicians use beats to tune instruments: when the beat frequency falls to zero, the two notes are in unison.

Worked example: Two tuning forks of 256 Hz and 260 Hz sounded together give |260 - 256| = 4 beats per second.

12.12 THE DOPPLER EFFECT

The DOPPLER EFFECT is the change in the OBSERVED (apparent) frequency of a wave when the source, the observer, or both are moving relative to the medium. The classic experience is the drop in pitch of a train whistle as it passes you. If v is the speed of sound in the medium, v_s the speed of the source and v_o the speed of the observer, and f the true frequency emitted, then the apparent frequency is

   f' = f (v +/- v_o) / (v -/+ v_s).

Sign convention (take the direction from source to observer as positive): use the signs that make f' INCREASE when source and observer approach each other and DECREASE when they recede.
 - Source approaching a stationary observer:  f' = f v/(v - v_s)  (pitch rises).
 - Source receding from a stationary observer: f' = f v/(v + v_s)  (pitch falls).
 - Observer approaching a stationary source:   f' = f (v + v_o)/v (pitch rises).
 - Observer receding from a stationary source:  f' = f (v - v_o)/v (pitch falls).

Worked example: A source of true frequency 500 Hz moves towards a stationary listener at 34 m/s in air where v = 340 m/s. The apparent frequency is f' = 500 x 340/(340 - 34) = 500 x 340/306 = 555.6 Hz - the pitch is raised. After it passes, f' = 500 x 340/(340 + 34) = 454.5 Hz, so the listener hears a sudden drop of about 100 Hz. The Doppler effect underlies radar speed guns, the red-shift of receding galaxies, and medical ultrasound blood-flow measurement.

SUMMARY

- A wave transports energy without transporting matter; mechanical waves need inertia and elasticity.
- Transverse waves vibrate perpendicular to propagation (crests/troughs); longitudinal waves vibrate along it (compressions/rarefactions).
- v = f lambda relates speed, frequency and wavelength; a progressive wave is y = A sin(omega t - k x) with omega = 2 pi f and k = 2 pi/lambda, so v = omega/k.
- Wave on a string: v = sqrt(T/mu). Sound in a gas: Newton v = sqrt(P/rho); Laplace's adiabatic correction gives the correct v = sqrt(gamma P/rho).
- Superposition: displacements add. Coherent waves interfere - constructive (in phase, path diff n lambda) or destructive (out of phase, path diff (n+1/2) lambda).
- Two opposite waves form a stationary wave y = 2A cos(kx) sin(omega t) with fixed nodes and antinodes (node-antinode spacing lambda/4).
- String fixed both ends and open pipe give ALL harmonics f_n = n f1; a closed pipe gives only ODD harmonics f_n = (2n-1) f1, with fundamental v/4L (an octave below the open pipe of equal length).
- Beats: f_beat = |f1 - f2|.
- Doppler effect: f' = f (v +/- v_o)/(v -/+ v_s); pitch rises on approach, falls on recession.

glossary.definition: A disturbance that travels through a medium or space, transporting energy and momentum without net transport of matter.
A wave in which particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation; shows crests and troughs.
A wave in which particles vibrate along the direction of propagation; shows compressions and rarefactions, e.g. sound.
The distance between two consecutive points of a wave that are in the same phase, such as crest to crest.
The number of complete oscillations per second, measured in hertz; f = 1/T.
The time taken for one complete oscillation of a particle of the medium.
The distance travelled by the disturbance per second; v = f lambda = omega/k.
The angular wave number k = 2 pi/lambda, measured in radians per metre.
The mass per unit length of a string, kg/m; it fixes the wave speed v = sqrt(T/mu).
The resultant displacement where waves overlap equals the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.
The steady reinforcement or cancellation produced when two coherent waves overlap; constructive or destructive.
A wave formed by two equal waves travelling in opposite directions; it has fixed nodes and antinodes and transports no energy.
A node is a point of zero amplitude in a stationary wave; an antinode is a point of maximum amplitude, midway between nodes.
The periodic rise and fall of loudness heard when two notes of slightly different frequency sound together; f_beat = |f1 - f2|.
The change in observed frequency of a wave due to relative motion of the source and/or observer through the medium.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Wave Phenomena (NIOS Senior Secondary Physics)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show working for numerical problems. Take the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s and pi = 3.1416 unless a value is given in the question.

questions.question: Distinguish between transverse and longitudinal waves, giving one example of each.
questions.answer:
In a TRANSVERSE wave the particles of the medium vibrate perpendicular to the direction the wave travels; it shows crests and troughs. Example: a wave on a stretched string (or light).
In a LONGITUDINAL wave the particles vibrate along (parallel to) the direction of travel; it shows compressions and rarefactions. Example: sound in air.
Transverse mechanical waves need a medium that supports shear (solids/surfaces); longitudinal waves travel through solids, liquids and gases.
questions.explanation: Direction of particle vibration relative to propagation, plus the crest/trough vs compression/rarefaction distinction.

questions.question: A wave y = 0.03 sin(400 t - 8 x) (SI units) travels along a string. Find its amplitude, angular frequency, wave number, wavelength, frequency and wave speed.
questions.answer:
Compare with y = A sin(omega t - k x).
Amplitude A = 0.03 m.
Angular frequency omega = 400 rad/s.
Wave number k = 8 rad/m.
Wavelength lambda = 2 pi/k = 2 x 3.1416/8 = 0.785 m.
Frequency f = omega/(2 pi) = 400/6.283 = 63.7 Hz.
Wave speed v = omega/k = 400/8 = 50 m/s (check: f lambda = 63.7 x 0.785 = 50 m/s).
questions.explanation: Read A, omega, k off the equation; then lambda = 2pi/k, f = omega/2pi, v = omega/k.

questions.question: A string of length 0.8 m has mass 16 g and is stretched to a tension of 100 N. Calculate the speed of a transverse wave on it.
questions.answer:
Linear mass density mu = mass/length = 0.016 kg / 0.8 m = 0.02 kg/m.
Wave speed v = sqrt(T/mu) = sqrt(100/0.02) = sqrt(5000) = 70.7 m/s.
questions.explanation: Compute mu = m/L, then apply v = sqrt(T/mu).

questions.question: State Newton's formula for the speed of sound in a gas and explain Laplace's correction.
questions.answer:
Newton assumed the compressions and rarefactions of sound occur isothermally, so the elasticity equals the pressure P and v = sqrt(P/rho). For air this gives about 280 m/s, roughly 15 percent below the measured 332 m/s.
Laplace pointed out that sound vibrations are so rapid that no heat flows - the process is ADIABATIC - so the effective elasticity is gamma P (gamma = C_p/C_v). Hence v = sqrt(gamma P/rho). With gamma = 1.40 for air this gives about 332 m/s, matching experiment.
questions.explanation: Newton isothermal v = sqrt(P/rho); Laplace adiabatic v = sqrt(gamma P/rho) corrects the ~15% error.

questions.question: State the principle of superposition and give the path-difference conditions for constructive and destructive interference.
questions.answer:
Principle of superposition: when two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement of a particle at any instant equals the algebraic (vector) sum of the displacements due to the individual waves; after crossing, each wave continues unchanged.
Constructive interference: waves in phase, path difference = n lambda (n = 0, 1, 2, ...); amplitudes add (max A1 + A2).
Destructive interference: waves out of phase by half a cycle, path difference = (n + 1/2) lambda; amplitudes subtract (min |A1 - A2|).
questions.explanation: Definition plus the two path-difference conditions.

questions.question: Explain how a stationary wave is formed and describe nodes and antinodes. Derive the fundamental frequency of a string fixed at both ends.
questions.answer:
When two progressive waves of equal amplitude and frequency travel in opposite directions and superpose - for example an incident wave and its reflection - a STATIONARY wave results. Adding y1 = A sin(omega t - k x) and y2 = A sin(omega t + k x) gives y = 2A cos(kx) sin(omega t). Each particle vibrates in SHM with an amplitude 2A cos(kx) that depends on position.
NODES are points where the amplitude is always zero (cos kx = 0), spaced lambda/2 apart; ANTINODES are points of maximum amplitude 2A, midway between the nodes. A node and the adjacent antinode are lambda/4 apart. No energy is transported past a node.
A string fixed at both ends must have a node at each end. In the fundamental (first harmonic) there is one antinode in the middle, so the length holds half a wavelength: L = lambda/2, i.e. lambda = 2L. Since v = sqrt(T/mu), the fundamental frequency is f1 = v/lambda = v/(2L) = (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu).
questions.explanation: Superpose opposite waves to get y = 2A cos(kx) sin(omega t); node/antinode definitions; L = lambda/2 gives f1 = (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu).

questions.question: Two tuning forks of frequencies 341 Hz and 345 Hz are sounded together. How many beats are heard per second? What happens if the 345 Hz fork is loaded slightly with wax?
questions.answer:
Beat frequency = |f1 - f2| = |345 - 341| = 4 beats per second.
Loading a fork with wax lowers its frequency. If the 345 Hz fork's frequency falls towards 341 Hz, the beat frequency decreases (fewer beats); if it falls below 341 Hz, the difference then grows again. So loading tells us which fork had the higher frequency by watching whether the beats slow down or speed up.
questions.explanation: f_beat = |f1 - f2| = 4 Hz; loading lowers frequency, changing the beat count.

questions.question: A closed organ pipe 0.34 m long is sounded in air where the speed of sound is 340 m/s. Find its fundamental frequency and the frequency of its first overtone.
questions.answer:
A closed pipe has fundamental f1 = v/(4L) = 340/(4 x 0.34) = 340/1.36 = 250 Hz.
A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics, so the first overtone is the third harmonic: f3 = 3 f1 = 3 x 250 = 750 Hz.
questions.explanation: Closed pipe: f1 = v/4L = 250 Hz; only odd harmonics, so first overtone = 3 f1 = 750 Hz.

questions.question: A car sounds a horn of frequency 400 Hz while moving towards a stationary observer at 20 m/s. Taking the speed of sound as 340 m/s, find the frequency heard by the observer.
questions.answer:
Source approaching a stationary observer: f' = f v/(v - v_s) = 400 x 340/(340 - 20) = 400 x 340/320 = 400 x 1.0625 = 425 Hz.
The observer hears a higher pitch, 425 Hz, because the source is approaching.
questions.explanation: Approaching source: f' = f v/(v - v_s) = 425 Hz.

questions.question: Compare an open pipe and a closed pipe of the same length: which harmonics does each produce, and how do their fundamental frequencies compare? Give the allowed-frequency formulae.
questions.answer:
OPEN PIPE (open at both ends): a displacement antinode at each end. The fundamental fits half a wavelength, L = lambda/2, so f1 = v/(2L). Allowed frequencies f_n = n v/(2L) with n = 1, 2, 3, ... - it produces ALL harmonics (odd and even).
CLOSED PIPE (closed at one end): a node at the closed end, antinode at the open end. The fundamental fits a quarter wavelength, L = lambda/4, so f1 = v/(4L). Allowed frequencies f_n = (2n - 1) v/(4L) = v/4L, 3v/4L, 5v/4L, ... - only ODD harmonics.
Comparison: for the same length L, the closed-pipe fundamental v/4L is exactly half the open-pipe fundamental v/2L, so a closed pipe sounds an OCTAVE LOWER. The open pipe is also richer in tone because it contains even harmonics that the closed pipe lacks.
questions.explanation: Open: all harmonics, f1 = v/2L. Closed: odd harmonics only, f1 = v/4L (an octave lower).

questions.question: A wave transports
options: matter from one point to another
energy without net transport of matter
both matter and energy in bulk
questions.answer: energy without net transport of matter
questions.explanation: A wave carries energy and momentum; the particles only oscillate about fixed mean positions.

questions.question: Two properties a medium must have to carry a mechanical wave are
questions.explanation: Inertia stores kinetic energy; elasticity supplies the restoring force.

questions.question: In a transverse wave the particles of the medium vibrate
options: perpendicular to the direction of propagation
questions.answer: perpendicular to the direction of propagation
questions.explanation: Transverse means particle motion is at right angles to the wave's travel.

questions.question: In a longitudinal wave the particles vibrate
options: parallel to the direction of propagation
questions.answer: parallel to the direction of propagation
questions.explanation: Longitudinal waves have particle motion along the direction of travel.

questions.question: Which of the following is a longitudinal wave?
options: A wave on a stretched string

questions.question: Why does Newton's formula for the speed of sound in air give a value about 15 percent too low?
questions.answer: Newton assumed the compressions and rarefactions of a sound wave happen isothermally (temperature constant), so the relevant elasticity is the pressure P and v = sqrt(P/rho) ~ 280 m/s. In reality the changes are so rapid that no heat can flow - the process is adiabatic - and the effective elasticity is gamma P, not P. Ignoring the factor gamma = 1.40 makes Newton's value low by a factor sqrt(1.40) ~ 1.18, i.e. about 15 percent.
questions.explanation: Newton's isothermal assumption misses the factor gamma; correct process is adiabatic.

questions.question: Write Laplace's formula for the speed of sound in a gas and show it predicts about 332 m/s for air.

questions.question: State the principle of superposition of waves.
questions.answer: When two or more waves travel through the same region simultaneously, the resultant displacement of any particle at any instant is the algebraic (vector) sum of the displacements that each wave would produce individually. After they cross, each wave continues on unchanged, as if the others had not been present.
questions.explanation: Resultant = algebraic sum; waves emerge unchanged.

questions.question: State the conditions (in terms of path difference) for constructive and destructive interference.
questions.answer: Constructive interference (reinforcement): path difference = n lambda, where n = 0, 1, 2, ...; the waves arrive in phase and amplitudes add. Destructive interference (cancellation): path difference = (n + 1/2) lambda; the waves arrive out of phase by half a cycle and amplitudes subtract.
questions.explanation: Constructive: n lambda; destructive: (n+1/2) lambda.

questions.question: Does interference of waves violate the conservation of energy? Explain.
questions.answer: No. Interference does not create or destroy energy; it merely REDISTRIBUTES it. The energy that is 'missing' from the dark (destructive) regions reappears in the bright (constructive) regions, where the intensity is more than the simple sum. Averaged over the whole pattern, the total energy is exactly conserved.
questions.explanation: Energy is moved from dark to bright regions; total conserved.

questions.question: How is a stationary wave formed, and how does it differ from a progressive wave?

Differences: a progressive wave transports energy and every particle has the same amplitude; a stationary wave transports no net energy, has fixed nodes (zero amplitude) and antinodes (maximum amplitude), and the amplitude varies with position as 2A cos(kx).

questions.question: Explain, using the Doppler effect, why the pitch of an ambulance siren drops as it passes you.
questions.answer: As the ambulance approaches, the source moves towards you, so successive wavefronts are crowded closer together; the apparent frequency f' = f v/(v - v_s) is higher than the true frequency, giving a raised pitch. The instant it passes and starts receding, the wavefronts are stretched out and f' = f v/(v + v_s) is lower than the true frequency, so the pitch suddenly drops. The change happens as the relative motion reverses from approaching to receding.

questions.question: Define the terms amplitude, wavelength, frequency, time period and wave velocity, and derive the relation v = f lambda.
questions.answer:
AMPLITUDE (A): the maximum displacement of a particle from its mean position (metres); linked to energy (energy proportional to A^2).
WAVELENGTH (lambda): the distance between two consecutive points in the same phase, e.g. crest to crest (metres).
FREQUENCY (f): the number of complete oscillations per second (hertz); f = 1/T.
TIME PERIOD (T): the time for one complete oscillation (seconds).
WAVE VELOCITY (v): the distance the disturbance travels per second.
Derivation of v = f lambda: In exactly one time period T, every particle completes one oscillation and the wave pattern advances by exactly one wavelength lambda. Therefore v = distance/time = lambda/T. Since f = 1/T, we have v = lambda x (1/T) = f lambda. Thus the wave speed equals the product of frequency and wavelength.
questions.explanation: Define the five terms; use 'one wavelength per period' to get v = lambda/T = f lambda.

questions.question: Explain the origin of the progressive wave equation y = A sin(omega t - k x) and show that the wave speed is v = omega/k.
questions.answer: Consider a wave moving in the +x direction. Let the particle at x = 0 execute SHM: y(0, t) = A sin(omega t), where omega = 2 pi f. The disturbance reaches a particle at position x a time x/v later, so that particle repeats the same motion but delayed: y(x, t) = A sin[omega (t - x/v)] = A sin(omega t - (omega/v) x). Writing k = omega/v (the wave number), this becomes y(x, t) = A sin(omega t - k x). Since omega = 2 pi f and, over one period, a point of constant phase advances one wavelength, k = omega/v = 2 pi/lambda. Rearranging k = omega/v gives the wave speed v = omega/k = (2 pi f)/(2 pi/lambda) = f lambda. The term (omega t - k x) is the phase; a wave travelling in -x is y = A sin(omega t + k x).
questions.explanation: Time delay x/v gives y = A sin(omega(t - x/v)); with k = omega/v, v = omega/k = f lambda.

questions.question: Derive the speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string, v = sqrt(T/mu), and discuss how tension and linear mass density affect it.
questions.answer:
Consider a small element of a string of linear mass density mu (kg/m) under tension T, forming a small arc of a circle of radius R as a transverse pulse passes; in the frame moving with the pulse the element travels at speed v. The tension acting at the two ends of the arc provides the centripetal force. For a small arc subtending angle 2(theta), the net inward force is 2 T sin(theta) ~ 2 T theta = T (arc length)/R. The element's mass is mu x (arc length), so Newton's second law for circular motion gives T (arc length)/R = mu (arc length) v^2 / R. Cancelling (arc length)/R gives T = mu v^2, hence v = sqrt(T/mu).
Discussion: the speed rises with the square root of tension (a tighter string carries waves faster) and falls with the square root of the linear mass density (a heavier string carries them slower). It does NOT depend on the wave's frequency or amplitude - only on the string's own properties. This is why thin, tight strings sound higher than thick, slack ones.
questions.explanation: Centripetal-force argument gives T = mu v^2, so v = sqrt(T/mu); v proportional to sqrt(T), inverse sqrt(mu).

questions.question: State Newton's formula for the speed of sound in a gas, explain why it fails, and describe Laplace's correction with the reasoning behind it.
questions.answer:
Newton treated sound as an elastic wave, v = sqrt(E/rho), and assumed the compressions and rarefactions occur ISOTHERMALLY - slowly enough for heat to flow so the temperature stays constant. For an isothermal change the bulk elasticity of a gas equals its pressure P, giving Newton's formula v = sqrt(P/rho). For air this yields about 280 m/s.
Why it fails: the measured speed of sound in air is about 332 m/s, so Newton's value is roughly 15 percent too low. The error is too large to blame on experiment.
Laplace's correction: Laplace argued that a sound wave alternately compresses and rarefies the gas thousands of times per second, far too fast for any heat to flow in or out. The process is therefore ADIABATIC, not isothermal. For an adiabatic change the effective bulk elasticity is gamma P, where gamma = C_p/C_v is the ratio of the specific heats. Hence v = sqrt(gamma P/rho). For air gamma = 1.40, which raises the predicted speed by a factor sqrt(1.40) ~ 1.18 to about 332 m/s - in excellent agreement with experiment. Using P = rho R T/M this also gives v = sqrt(gamma R T/M), showing v depends on temperature but not on pressure.
questions.explanation: Newton isothermal v = sqrt(P/rho) ~280 m/s (too low); Laplace adiabatic v = sqrt(gamma P/rho) ~332 m/s.

questions.question: Explain interference of waves. State the conditions for constructive and destructive interference and show that energy is conserved.
questions.answer:
When two coherent waves (same frequency, constant phase difference) overlap, the principle of superposition gives a resultant whose amplitude depends on the phase difference between them. Where the waves are in phase they reinforce; where they are out of phase they cancel. The steady resulting pattern of alternating strong and weak regions is called INTERFERENCE.
Constructive interference: the waves arrive in phase, path difference = n lambda (n = 0, 1, 2, ...). The amplitudes add: resultant amplitude = A1 + A2, and since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, the intensity is a maximum (for equal amplitudes, four times that of one wave).
Destructive interference: the waves arrive out of phase by half a cycle, path difference = (n + 1/2) lambda. The amplitudes subtract: resultant amplitude = |A1 - A2| (zero if A1 = A2), giving minimum intensity.
Energy conservation: interference does not create or destroy energy. The energy apparently lost at the dark fringes is exactly the extra energy that appears at the bright fringes. If we average the intensity over a whole set of fringes, it equals the simple sum of the individual intensities, so the total energy is conserved - interference only REDISTRIBUTES energy in space.
questions.explanation: Coherent overlap; constructive n lambda (amplitudes add), destructive (n+1/2) lambda (subtract); energy redistributed, conserved.

questions.question: Describe the modes of vibration of a string fixed at both ends. Obtain the frequencies of the harmonics and explain harmonics and overtones.
questions.answer:
A string fixed at both ends must carry a stationary wave with a NODE at each fixed end. The allowed patterns fit an integer number of half-wavelengths between the ends: L = n lambda_n/2, so lambda_n = 2L/n for n = 1, 2, 3, .... Since the wave speed is v = sqrt(T/mu), the allowed frequencies are f_n = v/lambda_n = n v/(2L) = n (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu).
FUNDAMENTAL (n = 1): one antinode in the middle, L = lambda/2, f1 = (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu). This is the lowest note and the FIRST HARMONIC.
Higher modes: f2 = 2 f1 (two loops, SECOND harmonic = first OVERTONE); f3 = 3 f1 (third harmonic = second overtone), and so on.
Harmonics are the frequencies that are integer multiples of the fundamental (f_n = n f1). Overtones are the allowed frequencies ABOVE the fundamental, numbered separately: the first overtone is the second harmonic, the second overtone is the third harmonic, etc. A string fixed at both ends produces ALL integer harmonics, which gives it a rich musical tone.
questions.explanation: Nodes at both ends -> L = n lambda/2 -> f_n = n(1/2L)sqrt(T/mu); harmonics = n f1, overtones numbered above the fundamental.

questions.question: Compare the vibrations of an open pipe and a closed pipe. Derive the allowed frequencies of each and explain the difference in their harmonic content.
questions.answer:
OPEN PIPE (open at both ends): the air at each open end is free to move, so there is a displacement ANTINODE at each end. The fundamental fits half a wavelength between the ends: L = lambda/2, giving f1 = v/(2L). Fitting more half-wavelengths gives L = n lambda_n/2, so the allowed frequencies are f_n = n v/(2L) with n = 1, 2, 3, ... - ALL harmonics (odd and even) are present.
CLOSED PIPE (closed at one end, open at the other): the closed end forces a NODE (air cannot move there) and the open end is an ANTINODE. The shortest fit is a quarter wavelength: L = lambda/4, giving the fundamental f1 = v/(4L). The next possible fits are L = 3 lambda/4, 5 lambda/4, ..., i.e. L = (2n-1) lambda/4, so the allowed frequencies are f_n = (2n-1) v/(4L) = v/4L, 3v/4L, 5v/4L, ... - ONLY the ODD harmonics.
Difference: (i) An open pipe contains all harmonics while a closed pipe contains only odd harmonics, so the open pipe has a richer, fuller tone. (ii) For equal length, the closed-pipe fundamental v/4L is half the open-pipe fundamental v/2L, so a closed pipe sounds one octave lower than an open pipe of the same length.
questions.explanation: Open: antinodes both ends, f_n = n v/2L (all harmonics). Closed: node-antinode, f_n = (2n-1) v/4L (odd only); closed is an octave lower.

questions.question: Explain what a beat is and derive that the beat frequency equals the difference of the two source frequencies. Give one use of beats.
questions.answer:
When two notes of slightly different frequencies f1 and f2 (and nearly equal amplitude A) sound together, the principle of superposition gives a resultant that can be written y = 2A cos(2 pi ((f1 - f2)/2) t) cos(2 pi ((f1 + f2)/2) t). The second cosine is a rapid oscillation at the average frequency (f1 + f2)/2 - the pitch we hear - while the first cosine slowly MODULATES its amplitude. The loudness is greatest whenever cos(2 pi ((f1 - f2)/2) t) = +1 or -1, and it becomes maximum twice in each cycle of that slow term. Hence the number of loudness maxima (beats) per second is 2 x (f1 - f2)/2 = f1 - f2. Taking the magnitude, the BEAT FREQUENCY is f_beat = |f1 - f2|.
Beats are audible only when f1 and f2 are close (within about 10 Hz); otherwise the ear hears two separate notes. USE: musicians tune an instrument against a standard note by reducing the beats to zero, at which point the two are exactly in unison. Beats are also used to measure a small unknown frequency difference.
questions.explanation: Superpose two close frequencies -> amplitude modulated at (f1-f2)/2, two maxima per cycle -> f_beat = |f1 - f2|; used for tuning.

questions.question: A physics class studies a transverse wave travelling along a long rope. The wave is described by y = 0.04 sin(50 t - 2 x), where all quantities are in SI units. (a) State the amplitude and the wave number. (b) Find the wavelength and the frequency. (c) Calculate the wave speed. (d) What is the maximum speed of a point on the rope?
questions.answer: (a) Comparing with y = A sin(omega t - k x): amplitude A = 0.04 m; wave number k = 2 rad/m (and omega = 50 rad/s). (b) Wavelength lambda = 2 pi/k = 6.283/2 = 3.14 m; frequency f = omega/2 pi = 50/6.283 = 7.96 Hz. (c) Wave speed v = omega/k = 50/2 = 25 m/s (check: f lambda = 7.96 x 3.14 = 25 m/s). (d) Maximum particle speed = A omega = 0.04 x 50 = 2.0 m/s, which is much less than the wave speed.
questions.explanation: Read A, omega, k; lambda = 2pi/k, f = omega/2pi, v = omega/k, particle speed = A omega.

questions.question: A sonometer wire of length 1.0 m and mass 8.0 g is stretched by a tension of 200 N. (a) Find the linear mass density mu. (b) Find the speed of a transverse wave on the wire. (c) Find the fundamental frequency. (d) What happens to the fundamental frequency if the tension is made four times as large?
questions.answer: (a) mu = mass/length = 0.008 kg / 1.0 m = 0.008 kg/m. (b) v = sqrt(T/mu) = sqrt(200/0.008) = sqrt(25000) = 158.1 m/s. (c) Fundamental f1 = v/(2L) = 158.1/(2 x 1.0) = 79.1 Hz. (d) f1 proportional to sqrt(T); making T four times larger doubles v and hence doubles f1 to about 158 Hz.
questions.explanation: mu = m/L; v = sqrt(T/mu); f1 = v/2L; f1 proportional to sqrt(T).

questions.question: Sound travels through air. Newton predicted its speed using v = sqrt(P/rho), but the measured value differs. Take P = 1.0 x 10^5 Pa, rho = 1.29 kg/m^3 and gamma = 1.40 for air. (a) Compute Newton's predicted speed. (b) Compute Laplace's predicted speed. (c) Which is closer to the measured ~332 m/s? (d) What wrong assumption did Newton make?
questions.answer: (a) Newton: v = sqrt(P/rho) = sqrt(1.0 x 10^5 / 1.29) = sqrt(77519) = 278.4 m/s. (b) Laplace: v = sqrt(gamma P/rho) = sqrt(1.40 x 1.0 x 10^5 / 1.29) = sqrt(108527) = 329.4 m/s. (c) Laplace's value (~329 m/s) is much closer to the measured ~332 m/s. (d) Newton wrongly assumed the compressions and rarefactions are ISOTHERMAL; they are actually so rapid that they are ADIABATIC, which introduces the factor gamma.
questions.explanation: Newton ~278 m/s (isothermal, too low); Laplace ~329 m/s (adiabatic) matches; Newton's error was assuming isothermal.

questions.question: Two loudspeakers driven by the same oscillator emit sound of wavelength 0.5 m and reach a listener by paths of different lengths. (a) State the principle that lets us add the two waves. (b) If the path difference is 1.0 m, is the interference constructive or destructive? (c) If the path difference is 0.25 m, what do you hear? (d) Does interference create or destroy sound energy overall?
questions.answer: (a) The principle of superposition - the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the two waves. (b) Path difference 1.0 m = 2 x 0.5 m = 2 lambda, a whole number of wavelengths, so the interference is CONSTRUCTIVE (loud). (c) Path difference 0.25 m = lambda/4... check against (n+1/2)lambda = 0.25, 0.75, ...; 0.25 m = lambda/2 is NOT satisfied here since lambda/2 = 0.25 m, so 0.25 m = (0+1/2) lambda, which is DESTRUCTIVE - a faint or silent point. (d) No; interference only redistributes energy from quiet regions to loud regions - the total sound energy is conserved.
questions.explanation: Superposition; 2 lambda -> constructive; lambda/2 -> destructive; energy redistributed not destroyed.

questions.question: A stretched string is clamped at both ends and set vibrating so that a stationary wave forms. (a) What boundary condition must hold at each clamped end? (b) In the fundamental mode, how much of a wavelength fits on the string? (c) Write the formula for the n-th harmonic frequency. (d) Which harmonics can this string produce?
questions.answer: (a) Each clamped (fixed) end must be a NODE - a point of zero displacement. (b) In the fundamental there is one antinode in the middle, so exactly half a wavelength fits: L = lambda/2. (c) f_n = n v/(2L) = n (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu), for n = 1, 2, 3, .... (d) It can produce ALL integer harmonics (both odd and even), since every f_n = n f1 is allowed.
questions.explanation: Nodes at fixed ends; L = lambda/2; f_n = n v/2L; all harmonics.

questions.question: An organ has both open pipes and closed pipes. Take the speed of sound as 340 m/s. Consider an open pipe and a closed pipe each of length 0.5 m. (a) Find the fundamental frequency of the open pipe. (b) Find the fundamental frequency of the closed pipe. (c) By what factor do they differ? (d) List the first three allowed frequencies of the closed pipe.
questions.answer: (a) Open pipe: f1 = v/(2L) = 340/(2 x 0.5) = 340 Hz. (b) Closed pipe: f1 = v/(4L) = 340/(4 x 0.5) = 170 Hz. (c) The open-pipe fundamental (340 Hz) is twice the closed-pipe fundamental (170 Hz) - a factor of 2, i.e. one octave. (d) A closed pipe gives only odd harmonics: 170 Hz, 3 x 170 = 510 Hz, 5 x 170 = 850 Hz.
questions.explanation: Open f1 = v/2L = 340 Hz; closed f1 = v/4L = 170 Hz; ratio 2; closed frequencies 170, 510, 850 Hz.

questions.question: A student tunes a guitar using a 440 Hz reference tuning fork. When she plucks a string and sounds the fork together, she hears 3 beats per second. (a) What is the beat frequency? (b) What are the two possible frequencies of the string? (c) She slightly loosens the string and the beats increase to 5 per second. What was the original string frequency? (d) State the beat-frequency formula.
questions.answer: (a) The beat frequency is 3 Hz. (b) The string differs from 440 Hz by 3 Hz, so it is either 443 Hz or 437 Hz. (c) Loosening the string LOWERS its frequency. Since the beats increased (from 3 to 5), the string must have been BELOW the fork - loosening it further from 437 Hz increases the difference. So the original frequency was 437 Hz. (d) f_beat = |f1 - f2|.
questions.explanation: Beat freq 3 Hz; string 437 or 443 Hz; loosening increases beats so it was 437 Hz; f_beat = |f1 - f2|.

questions.question: A train sounds a horn of frequency 500 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m/s and the train moves at 34 m/s. (a) Find the frequency heard by a stationary observer as the train approaches. (b) Find the frequency heard as the train recedes. (c) By how much does the pitch change as the train passes? (d) Name the phenomenon.
questions.answer: (a) Approaching source: f' = f v/(v - v_s) = 500 x 340/(340 - 34) = 500 x 340/306 = 555.6 Hz. (b) Receding source: f' = f v/(v + v_s) = 500 x 340/(340 + 34) = 500 x 340/374 = 454.5 Hz. (c) The pitch drops by 555.6 - 454.5 = 101.1 Hz as the train passes. (d) This is the DOPPLER EFFECT.
questions.explanation: Approach f' = 555.6 Hz, recede f' = 454.5 Hz, drop ~101 Hz; the Doppler effect.

questions.question: A wave pulse travels along a rope and meets a second, identical pulse coming the other way. Consider the moment they overlap. (a) Which principle predicts the shape while they overlap? (b) If the pulses are on the same side of the rope, what is the resultant at the instant of complete overlap? (c) If they are on opposite sides, what is the resultant at that instant? (d) After they separate, how do the pulses look?
questions.answer: (a) The principle of superposition - add the displacements point by point. (b) If both pulses are on the same side (same sign), they add constructively; at complete overlap the resultant displacement is doubled (2A at the centre). (c) If they are on opposite sides (opposite signs and equal size), they cancel; at complete overlap the rope is momentarily straight (zero displacement everywhere), though the particles are still moving. (d) After they separate, each pulse continues unchanged in shape, size and speed, as if the other had never been there.
questions.explanation: Superposition; same side -> doubled; opposite -> cancel momentarily; pulses emerge unchanged.

questions.question: A whistle emits sound of frequency 680 Hz in air where sound travels at 340 m/s. (a) Find the wavelength of the sound. (b) An observer runs towards the stationary whistle at 17 m/s; find the frequency he hears. (c) Would he hear a higher or lower pitch? (d) If instead he ran away at the same speed, what frequency would he hear?
questions.answer: (a) lambda = v/f = 340/680 = 0.5 m. (b) Observer approaching a stationary source: f' = f (v + v_o)/v = 680 x (340 + 17)/340 = 680 x 357/340 = 714 Hz. (c) He hears a HIGHER pitch because he is moving towards the source. (d) Observer receding: f' = f (v - v_o)/v = 680 x (340 - 17)/340 = 680 x 323/340 = 646 Hz - a lower pitch.
questions.explanation: lambda = 0.5 m; approaching observer f' = 714 Hz (higher); receding f' = 646 Hz (lower).
